A1.notes.Q3: Course grades are essential for us to spot struggling students, but Absalon tracking feels like constant surveillance without enough immediate benefit.
A1.notes.Q4: Students need to know exactly why they are flagged so we can tailor our support correctly; otherwise, trust is lost.
A1.notes.Q5: We shouldn't disadvantage specific groups just to boost overall numbers, but balancing false positives across all groups seems fairer.
A1.notes.Q6: A one-time email might get lost; if a flag goes up, we need to reach the student immediately rather than waiting.
A1.notes.Q7: With personalized outreach from advisors, privacy concerns are higher, so I prefer being more selective and avoiding unnecessary false alarms.

A2.notes.Q3:
High school GPA feels invasive compared to actual grades; it's a proxy, not the real data I use daily.
Disability info is sensitive but crucial for access - if we get +5 accurate flags here worth doing.
Online clicks (Q3.4) terrify me as privacy vs no answer.
A2.notes.Q4:
My role relies on talking to students, not just an alert text.
Need clear reasons so they trust the warning and don't deny it.
Can accept lower explainability only if accuracy jump is massive (>5%).
Very low makes me feel like a detective with no clues.
A2.notes.Q5:
Fairness must equalize how well we catch genuine struggles (recall) and avoid flagging healthy students unfairly.
False positives are costly - they waste time on non-needing students.
I'd rather miss a few than harass good performers who don't need help.
A2.notes.Q6:
Emails alone feel dismissive for 'at risk' students.
I think personalized outreach works best but carries stigma risks if not careful.
Continuously vs once a year? Depends on how the flag behaves over time.
A2.notes.Q7:
For general emails, casting a wide net is acceptable as long as it doesn't clog inboxes.
But with personalized suggestions based on behavior? I'd worry about triggering defensive reactions and missing the human element.
A2.Q8.1:
The biggest gap is that students often hide difficulties due to stigma until they are already far behind, making early intervention harder than models predict.

Also, no one has considered how advisors themselves feel when receiving these automated alerts daily - could lead to alert fatigue and burnout affecting the human support quality.

A3.Q8.1: We need to ensure that the model doesn't create new forms of stigma for first-gen students who might feel they are being 'targeted' rather than helped.

S1.notes.Q3: I've dropped out twice, so knowing my history helps me get help earlier. But using gender or race feels wrong unless it actually removes bias I'm seeing today.
S1.notes.Q4: I need to know why I'm flagged so I can fight it if needed, but for a model that misses me sometimes, even low explainability might be okay.
S1.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial because society treats some groups worse than others; missing support there hurts them most.
S1.notes.Q6: If the system flags me, I want help immediately. Being contacted yearly is too slow when you're in crisis.
S1.notes.Q7: Personalized emails are very intrusive. If I don't actually struggle, this feels like bullying rather than support.

S2.notes.Q3: Course grades are relevant but high school GPA feels invasive without direct academic data from me right now.
S2.notes.Q4: I need to understand exactly why I'm flagged so the advisor knows where to help, not just 'pattern detected'.
S2.notes.Q5: Missing students from my background is risky; false positives waste time but are okay if they don't harm.
S2.notes.Q6: Since I work part-time, a quick personalized email would be best, but immediate action is crucial.
S2.notes.Q7: Personalized emails feel like surveillance; fewer people should get flagged unless I'm actually struggling.

S3.notes.Q3: My disability data is crucial for me, but I need strong proof that it helps before agreeing to share more sensitive info like race or age.
S3.notes.Q4: I need to understand exactly why I am flagged because it affects my mental health. A black box scares me.
S3.notes.Q5: Fairness matters, but contacting innocent people is worse than missing a few cases that we can catch later manually.
S3.notes.Q6: If the system detects I'm struggling, it needs to know immediately regardless of when that happens this semester.
S3.notes.Q7: General emails are okay for outreach; personalized ones feel intrusive unless the model is very certain.

S4.notes.Q3: Online activity feels like surveillance; grades and history are already visible but need better impact thresholds.
S4.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I'm flagged because it makes me anxious and defensive without a simple explanation.
S4.notes.Q5: We shouldn't miss anyone at the cost of unfairness, but fairness isn't worth letting good people suffer silently due to bias.
S4.notes.Q6: Given my ADHD and past dropout, waiting is dangerous. Personalization builds trust better than generic emails or meetings.
S4.notes.Q7: With a personalized email, I care more about being right because false positives feel like wasting time and resources for me personally.

S5.notes.Q3: Using grades makes sense since I struggled with the grading system here before, but nationality and gender feel too invasive for prediction unless it helps fairness specifically.
S5.notes.Q4: I need to understand exactly why I'm being flagged so it's not just 'the algorithm said so'. Simple rules like credit totals are easier for advisors and students to trust.
S5.notes.Q5: As an international student, I fear the model might misunderstand my struggles if it doesn't work well for people like me. Missing someone who needs help is worse than a false alarm.
S5.notes.Q6: A simple generic email feels too detached given my situation. Being proactive now is better than waiting until I fail completely.
S5.notes.Q7: With a personalized message, it's okay to reach out more broadly because the outreach itself feels supportive and less like surveillance if tailored correctly.

S6.notes.Q3: I've dropped out twice already; I can't afford to be ignored if the model works for me without invasive data like nationality or race.
S6.notes.Q4: If they flag me, I need to know exactly why so I can ask for help properly, but if it saves many lives at the cost of explanation, maybe that's okay.
S6.notes.Q5: It feels unfair if my group gets fewer opportunities just because I'm foreign or female; missing support for others is worse than missing me once in a blue moon.
S6.notes.Q6: A general email might not trigger action; if I'm struggling silently, getting specific help sooner is the only thing that could save my degree.
S6.notes.Q7: For a generic email, spamming people feels useless; for personalized ones hitting too few misses potential cases like me who need advocacy.

S7.notes.Q3: Grades matter for me to know if I'm struggling, but Absalon data feels like surveillance of my behavior. Sensitive data about disability is crucial given my status; accuracy must be high here.
S7.notes.Q4: As a dyslexic student, knowing *why* I'm flagged is vital for me to advocate correctly. Black box models are unacceptable; trust requires clarity.
S7.notes.Q5: I want support where it's needed, not just fair distribution that dilutes the total help available to everyone struggling academically.
S7.notes.Q6: Early intervention saves time for me with accommodations. I need immediate feedback if my patterns shift, not an annual check-up.
S7.notes.Q7: General emails are good but impersonal; personalized ones can be intrusive unless carefully targeted to avoid wasting advisor time on those who might not need help yet.

S8.notes.Q3: Course grades help me if I'm struggling, so that's okay with a moderate improvement needed. Admissions data feels irrelevant to current struggle but invasive enough for 'large' only. Absalon browsing is too intrusive; I wouldn't want it unless we catch everyone (never). Age and nationality are sensitive proxies—only age needs small gain. Disability info should be used if found without burden.
S8.notes.Q4: I want to know exactly why I'm flagged, not just a 'pattern detected'. I'd accept much lower explainability (low or very low) only if the model finds significantly more students than my current situation allowed.
S8.notes.Q5: Being missed is hard when you need help. I'd accept losing 3-people accuracy per group if it helps marginalized peers like me. We must catch those we miss, not just avoid false alarms.
S8.notes.Q6: I prefer generic emails first to reduce stigma; personal meetings later if there's a red flag. Frequent checks feel stressful unless clearly targeted, so annual or per-alert is better than continuous spam.
S8.notes.Q7: For simple generic tips, I can accept some noise (balancing). But for personalized advice, false alarms hurt more—strictly fewer students to avoid unwanted attention.
S8.Q8.1: As a dropout survivor, I fear the model might label anyone who misses one deadline as 'high risk', leading to stigmatization rather than support.

S9.notes.Q3: I feel very vulnerable right now with my mental health condition and disability. High-school GPA feels too invasive (prior to studying here). Online activity data feels like surveillance that could trigger stigma before I even get help.
S9.notes.Q5: It's hard to be fair when we have fewer resources per student due to my slow pace, but missing others is worse.
S9.notes.Q6: Continuous support might feel overwhelming if I don't need it right now, but early outreach is what kept me in this degree last time.
S9.notes.Q7: General info for everyone seems okay (less intrusive). Personalized emails help when I really struggle, so balance fits best there to avoid unnecessary anxiety.
S9.Q8.1: I'm worried the system might flag me if my progress slows again due to burnout or mental health fluctuations that aren't just academic performance issues.
